text: The 1972 Republican National Convention took place from August 21 to August 23, 1972, at the Miami Beach Convention Center in Miami Beach, Florida. It nominated then President Richard Nixon and then Vice President Spiro Agnew for reelection. The convention was chaired by House minority leader and future Nixon successor Gerald Ford of Michigan. This was the fifth time Nixon had been nominated on the Republican ticket for vice president (in the 1952 and 1956 United States presidential elections) or president (in the 1960 and 1968 United States presidential elections), with his five appearances matching the major-party standard set by Franklin D. Roosevelt, a Democrat who had been nominated for vice president once (in the 1920 United States presidential election) and president four times (in the 1932, 1936, 1940, and 1944 United States presidential elections). Nixon was the first Republican to be nominated three times for president. The convention was the first Republican convention scheduled for only three days since 1944 and, along with the 2012 Democratic National Convention, remains the only three-day conventions in modern history. Originally, San Diego, California, was selected as the host city on July 23, 1971, with the event planned for the San Diego Sports Arena. Columnist Jack Anderson uncovered a memo from Dita Beard, a lobbyist for the International Telephone and Telegraph Corp., indicating that ITT could pledge $400,000 for the San Diego bid if the Department of Justice settled its antitrust case against ITT. Fearing scandal and citing labor and cost concerns, the GOP moved the convention—just months before it was to begin—to Miami Beach, Florida, which also hosted the Democratic National Convention. This marked the sixth and final time both national party conventions were held in the same city; Chicago had hosted double conventions in 1884, 1932, 1944, and 1952, and Philadelphia in 1948. The Republican convention did not return to San Diego until 1996. The convention set a new standard as it was scripted as a media event to an unprecedented degree. Anne Armstrong of Texas delivered the first national convention keynote address by a woman. First Lady Pat Nixon became the first Republican First Lady and the first First Lady in over 25 years to address a party's national convention; her speech established a precedent followed by Republican First Ladies Nancy Reagan, Barbara Bush, Laura Bush, and Melania Trump, as well as Democratic First Ladies Hillary Clinton, Michelle Obama, and Jill Biden. Nixon easily defeated primary challenges from Representative John M. Ashbrook of Ohio (on the right) and Representative Pete McCloskey of California (on the left); however, under New Mexico state law, McCloskey earned one delegate, which the convention refused to seat, fearing he might nominate himself and deliver an anti-war speech. Congressman Manuel Lujan of New Mexico, a strong Nixon supporter, honored state law by voting for McCloskey. The final vote was 1,347 for Nixon, one for McCloskey, and none for Ashbrook. Throughout the precisely scripted convention, delegates repeatedly chanted "Four more years! Four more years!" Spiro Agnew was renominated for vice president with 1,345 votes, one vote for NBC television journalist David Brinkley, and two abstentions. The convention was expected to face widespread protests, particularly against the Vietnam War, and the Nixon administration made efforts to suppress them. This tension was documented by Top Value Television in the independent film *Four More Years*, which juxtaposed protest footage outside the convention with internal political proceedings. The next day, *The New York Times* reported that 900 demonstrators had been arrested and that 52 people, including 12 police officers, had been injured. In 2005, files released under a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit revealed that the Federal Bureau of Investigation monitored former Beatle John Lennon after he was invited to perform at Yippie protests; the surveillance concluded he was not a dangerous revolutionary, as he was "constantly under the influence of narcotics." The Justice Department indicted Scott Camil, John Kniffen, Alton Foss, Donald Perdue, William Patterson, Stan Michelsen, Peter Mahoney, and John Briggs—collectively known as the Gainesville Eight—for conspiracy to disrupt the convention, but all were exonerated. Oliver Stone's film *Born on the Fourth of July*, based on Ron Kovic's autobiography, depicts Kovic and fellow Vietnam Veterans Against the War activists Bobby Muller, Bill Wieman, and Mark Clevinger being spat upon at the convention. This scene did not appear in Kovic's autobiography but was adapted directly from a 1972 documentary titled *Operation Last Patrol*, created by filmmaker and actor Frank Cavestani and photo journalist Catherine Leroy.
